title: Keep reading until it stops

prereqs.why: The whole problem is reading an unknown number of values, which is what a while loop over std::cin is for.
A while loop is the right shape when you do not know the count in advance.

statement:
Read integers one at a time until you read a **0**, or until the input runs
out. Print the sum of everything read **before** the 0, then the count.

```
input:   4 9 2 0        input:   0           input:   5 5 5
output:  sum 15         output:  sum 0       output:  sum 15
         count 3                 count 0             count 3
```

The 0 itself is a **sentinel** — a marker that means "stop" — so it is not part
of the sum and not counted.

### The point of the problem

A `for` loop is for when you know the count. Here you do not: the input decides
when to stop. That is a `while`.

Two conditions end the loop, and both must work:

```cpp
int x{};
while (std::cin >> x && x != 0)
{
    // ...
}
```

`std::cin >> x` returns the stream, and a stream converts to `false` when the
read failed — because the input ended, or because what was there was not a
number. So that one expression handles "ran out of input" and the `&& x != 0`
handles the sentinel. Written the other way round it would test `x` before
reading into it.

### Boundary cases

A leading `0` means sum 0 and count 0. Input that ends with no `0` at all must
still print the totals rather than hanging or losing the last value. Negative
values count normally and can make the sum negative. The sums fit in an `int`.
hints: `while (std::cin >> x && x != 0)` does both jobs: the extraction is the first condition, and && short-circuits so `x != 0` is only checked once a value was actually read.
Declare the accumulator and the counter before the loop, both brace-initialised to zero, and add to them inside it.
Trace `0` on its own: the extraction succeeds, `x != 0` is false, the body never runs, and you print the zeros you started with. That is the case to get right first.
